title: Bending Moment in Elastic Beams
short_intro: The bending moment at any cross-section of a beam is the internal internal couple resulting from shearing stresses that resists external loads. It governs the curvature and structural deformation of beams under transverse loading.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of bending moment, relation with radius of curvature, internal elastic couples, and simple beam bending formulas.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Geometrical moment of inertia for various cross-sections, differential equation of the elastic curve, cantilever deflection, and loaded beams supported at ends.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Nature of Bending Moment
bullets: The bending moment at a section of a beam is equal to the algebraic sum of the moments of all forces acting on either side of the section.
It acts as an internal couple balancing the moment of external loads to maintain static and rotational equilibrium.

In a symmetrically bent beam, the upper fibers experience longitudinal tension (or compression) while the lower fibers experience the opposite, with a neutral layer undergoing zero longitudinal strain.

concept_notes.heading: Neutral Axis and Neutral Surface
bullets: The neutral surface is the longitudinal layer within the beam that undergoes neither extension nor compression during bending.
The intersection of the neutral surface with any transverse cross-section is called the neutral axis.
For beams of uniform symmetrical cross-section subjected to pure bending, the neutral axis passes through the centroid of the cross-section.

concept_notes.heading: Geometrical Moment of Inertia (Flexural Rigidity)
bullets: The flexural rigidity of a beam is given by the product Y I, where Y is Young's modulus and I is the geometrical moment of inertia of the cross-section about the neutral axis.
For a rectangular cross-section of breadth b and depth d, the geometrical moment of inertia is I = (bd³)/12.
For a circular cross-section of radius r, the geometrical moment of inertia about the diametral axis is I = (πr&sup4;)/4.

concept_notes.heading: Internal Bending Moment and Radius of Curvature
bullets: The internal bending moment M developed in a beam is directly proportional to its geometrical moment of inertia and inversely proportional to the radius of curvature R of the neutral axis.
The relation is expressed as M = (Y I)/R.
Greater flexural rigidity (Y I) results in a smaller curvature (larger radius R) for a given applied bending moment.

derivations.title: Relation Between Bending Moment and Radius of Curvature
derivations.conditions: Pure bending of a beam of uniform cross-section, elastic limit not exceeded, plane cross-sections remain plane after bending.
steps: Consider a small segment of length dx of a beam bent into an arc of a circle of radius R subtending an angle θ, such that dx = R θ.
Consider a longitudinal filament at a distance y from the neutral axis. Its original length is dx = R θ, and its stretched length is l' = (R + y)θ.
The longitudinal strain in this filament is ε = (l' - dx)/dx = ((R + y)θ - Rθ)/(Rθ) = y/R.
By Hooke's law, the longitudinal stress in the filament is σ = Y ε = (Y y)/R.
The tensile or compressive force acting on an elemental area dA at distance y is dF = σ dA = (Y / R) y dA.
The moment of this force about the neutral axis is dM = dF · y = (Y / R) y² dA.
Integrating over the entire cross-section, the total internal bending moment is M = ∫ dM = (Y / R) ∫ y² dA.
Recognizing that I = ∫ y² dA is the geometrical moment of inertia, we get M = (Y I) / R.

derivations.title: Elevation of a Cantilever Loaded at the Free End
derivations.conditions: Cantilever of length L, uniform rectangular cross-section (breadth b, depth d), loaded with a concentrated weight W at the free end.
steps: Consider a cantilever fixed at x = 0 and loaded with weight W at the free end x = L.
At a distance x from the fixed end, the bending moment due to the load W is M = W(L - x).
Equating this to the elastic bending moment, W(L - x) = (Y I)/R.
Using the small slope approximation where 1/R ≈ d²y/dx², the differential equation becomes Y I (d²y/dx²) = W(L - x).
Integrating once with respect to x using boundary conditions (dy/dx = 0 at x = 0), we find the slope dy/dx = (W / Y I)(Lx - x²/2).
Integrating again with respect to x using the boundary condition (y = 0 at x = 0), we obtain the deflection equation y = (W / Y I)(Lx²/2 - x³/6).
The maximum depression at the free end (x = L) is obtained by substituting x = L.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Bending of a Cantilever (Depression vs. Load)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of depression (δ) on the vertical axis versus applied load (W) on the horizontal axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The linear relationship confirms Hooke's law in bending; the slope of the line determines the experimental value of Young's modulus (Y).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in viva and numerical problems to calculate Young's modulus or depression.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Bending Stress Distribution Across Cross-Section
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A triangular stress distribution diagram across the depth of a rectangular beam showing zero stress at the neutral axis and maximum tensile/compressive stress at the outer fibers.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Stress varies linearly with distance from the neutral axis, justifying the use of outer material to bear maximum structural loads.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding stress magnitude at the neutral axis versus outer edges.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Elastic Curve of a Cantilever

graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents the vertical displacement y as a function of horizontal position x along the cantilever span.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT derivations for slope and deflection differential equations.

solved_numericals.question: A metal rod of rectangular cross-section with breadth 2 cm and depth 3 cm is bent by a couple. If Young's modulus of the material is 2 x 10^11 N/m^2 and the radius of curvature is 100 m, calculate the internal bending moment.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: b = 0.02 m, d = 0.03 m, Y = 2 × 10^11 N/m^2, R = 100 m.
Calculate the geometrical moment of inertia I = (b d^3) / 12 = (0.02 × (0.03)^3) / 12 = (0.02 × 2.7 × 10^-5) / 12 = 4.5 × 10^-8 m^4.
Substitute values into the bending moment formula: M = (Y I) / R = (2 × 10^11 × 4.5 × 10^-8) / 100.

solved_numericals.question: A cantilever of length 1.5 m has a rectangular cross-section of breadth 0.04 m and depth 0.02 m. A mass of 2 kg is suspended at its free end. Given g = 9.8 m/s^2 and Young's modulus Y = 1.0 x 10^11 N/m^2, calculate the depression at the free end.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 1.5 m, b = 0.04 m, d = 0.02 m, W = m g = 2 × 9.8 = 19.6 N, Y = 1.0 × 10^11 N/m^2.
Calculate geometrical moment of inertia I = (b d^3) / 12 = (0.04 × (0.02)^3) / 12 = (0.04 × 8 × 10^-6) / 12 = 2.67 × 10^-8 m^4.
Use the cantilever depression formula: δ = (W L^3) / (3 Y I).

solved_numericals.question: Two beams of the same material and mass have identical lengths. Beam A has a square cross-section of side a, while Beam B has a rectangular cross-section with depth 2a and breadth a/2. Compare their flexural rigidities.
solution_steps: For Beam A (square cross-section of side a): Moment of inertia I_A = (a × a^3) / 12 = a^4 / 12.
For Beam B (breadth b = a/2, depth d = 2a): Moment of inertia I_B = ((a/2) × (2a)^3) / 12 = ((a/2) × 8a^3) / 12 = (4a^4) / 12 = a^4 / 3.
Flexural rigidity ratio is given by (FR)_A / (FR)_B = (Y I_A) / (Y I_B) = I_A / I_B.
solved_numericals.answer: Flexural rigidity of Beam B is 4 times that of Beam A (FR_A : FR_B = 1 : 4)

assumptions_and_limitations: The material of the beam is homogeneous, isotropic, and obeys Hooke's law strictly.
Plane transverse sections before bending remain plane after bending (Bernoulli-Euler hypothesis).
The radius of curvature of the bent beam is very large compared to the transverse dimensions of the cross-section.
Deformations are small, permitting the approximation 1/R = d²y/dx².

common_misconceptions.wrong: The neutral axis experiences maximum tensile stress during bending.
common_misconceptions.correct: The neutral axis experiences zero stress and zero strain during bending.
common_misconceptions.why: The neutral layer lies at the center where longitudinal stretching and compression transition into one another.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Bending moment depends only on the applied force, not on the shape of the cross-section.
common_misconceptions.correct: Internal bending moment balances the external couple and depends directly on the geometrical moment of inertia of the cross-section.
common_misconceptions.why: Cross-sectional geometry (such as I-beams) significantly dictates how a beam resists bending for a given load.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Depression of a cantilever is directly proportional to the fourth power of its length.
common_misconceptions.correct: Depression is directly proportional to the cube of its length (δ ∝ L³).
common_misconceptions.why: Dimensional analysis and exact integration of the differential equation yield an L³ dependence.

quick_revision: Bending moment M is related to radius of curvature R by M = Y I / R.
Geometrical moment of inertia for a rectangular beam is I = bd³/12.
Flexural rigidity is the product of Young's modulus and geometrical moment of inertia (Y I).
Depression of a loaded cantilever varies directly as L³ and inversely as Y I.
